provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Revision of sss two work
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to solve algebraic expressions accurately.
The students should be able to identify geometric properties in given figures.
Introduction:
We will start by reviewing what we learned last year in algebra and geometry.
This revision will help us build a strong foundation for this term's topics.
Content:
Algebra involves solving equations and simplifying expressions.
For example, 2x + 5 = 15 can be solved to find x = 5.
Geometry deals with shapes, sizes, and properties of space.
In Nigeria, market traders use geometry to arrange their goods in triangular patterns for better display.
Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to solve algebraic problems and identify geometric properties in diagrams.
Evaluation questions:
Simplify the expression: 3x + 2x - 5x + 7
State the properties of a rectangle.
If a bag contains 5 green balls and 3 red balls, what is the probability of picking a green ball?
Summary:
Today's revision covered key algebraic and geometric concepts from SSS 2.
Students should practice these regularly to maintain their skills.

topics.title: Indices and logarithms
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the laws of indices.
The students should be able to solve logarithmic equations.
Introduction:
We have previously worked with numbers and operations.
Today we will extend this to indices and logarithms which are essential in advanced mathematics.
Content:
Indices represent repeated multiplication of a number.
The laws of indices include a^m × a^n = a^(m+n) and (a^m)^n = a^(mn).
For example, 2^3 × 2^4 = 2^(3+4) = 2^7 = 128.
Logarithms are the inverse of exponential functions.
The common logarithm uses base 10, written as log₁₀.
In Nigeria, when we say something costs 10^3 naira, we mean it costs 1000 naira.
Class activity:
Students will solve problems involving indices and logarithms using both theoretical and practical examples.
Evaluation questions:
State the three laws of indices.
Simplify: 3^2 × 3^4 ÷ 3^3
If log₂(x) = 3, find the value of x.
Solve the equation: log₃(2x + 1) = 2
Summary:
Indices and logarithms are fundamental mathematical concepts with applications in various fields.

topics.title: Surds
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to simplify surds.
The students should be able to rationalize denominators involving surds.
Introduction:
We have previously worked with integers and rational numbers.
Today we will explore irrational numbers called surds which appear in many mathematical problems.
Content:
Surds are irrational numbers expressed as roots.
For example, √2 and √7 are surds because they cannot be simplified to whole numbers.
To simplify surds, we look for perfect square factors.
For instance, √50 = √(25×2) = 5√2.
Rationalizing denominators involves removing surds from the bottom of fractions.
For example, to rationalize 1/√3, we multiply numerator and denominator by √3 to get √3/3.
In Nigeria, when measuring the diagonal of a square room, we often get surd values.
Class activity:
Students will practice simplifying various surds and rationalizing denominators in pairs.
Evaluation questions:
Simplify √72.
Rationalize the denominator of 2/√5.
Express √48 in its simplest form.
If √x = 2√3, find the value of x.
Summary:
Surds are irrational numbers that require special techniques for simplification and rationalization.

topics.title: Quadratic equations
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to solve quadratic equations using the formula.
The students should be able to solve word problems involving quadratic equations.
Introduction:
We have previously worked with linear equations.
Today we will extend our knowledge to quadratic equations which appear in many real-life situations.
Content:
Quadratic equations are polynomial equations of degree 2.
They can be written in the form ax² + bx + c = 0 where a, b, c are constants and a ≠ 0.
The quadratic formula is x = [-b ± √(b² - 4ac)] / 2a.
For example, to solve x² - 5x + 6 = 0, we get x = [5 ± √(25-24)]/2 = [5 ± 1]/2, so x = 3 or x = 2.
Completing the square involves rewriting x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² - (b/2)² + c.
Word problems might involve areas, distances, or profits.
For instance, if a farmer's rectangular field has an area of 200m² and one side is 10m longer than the other, we can set up a quadratic equation to find the dimensions.
Class activity:
Students will solve quadratic equations using both the formula and completing the square method.
Evaluation questions:
Solve the quadratic equation: x² - 7x + 10 = 0.
Use completing the square to solve: x² + 6x - 7 = 0.
A rectangle has an area of 24cm² and its length is 2cm more than its width. Find the dimensions.
The product of two consecutive numbers is 156. Find the numbers.
Summary:
Quadratic equations can be solved using the formula or by completing the square, and have applications in various real-world problems.

topics.title: Simultaneous equations
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to solve linear simultaneous equations.
The students should be able to solve one linear and one quadratic simultaneous equations.
Introduction:
We have previously worked with single equations.
Today we will learn how to solve systems of equations that must be satisfied simultaneously.
Content:
Simultaneous equations are equations that share common variables and must be true at the same time.
For two linear equations, we can use substitution or elimination methods.
For example, to solve x + y = 10 and 2x - y = 5, we can add them to get 3x = 15, so x = 5, then y = 5.
When one equation is linear and one is quadratic, we can substitute the linear into the quadratic.
For instance, with y = 2x and x² + y² = 20, we substitute to get x² + (2x)² = 20, so 5x² = 20, x² = 4, x = ±2.
In Nigeria, market traders might use simultaneous equations to determine the cost of different items when given total costs.
Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to solve various systems of equations, both linear and mixed.
Evaluation questions:
Solve the system: 2x + y = 11 and x - y = 2.
Find the values of x and y that satisfy both equations: y = x² and y = 2x + 3.
If 3 oranges and 2 mangoes cost ₦650, and 2 oranges and 3 mangoes cost ₦700, find the cost of one orange and one mango.
Solve: x + y = 7 and xy = 12.
Summary:
Simultaneous equations have multiple solutions that satisfy all equations in the system at once.

topics.title: Trigonometry: sine rule
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the sine rule.
The students should be able to apply the sine rule to solve triangle problems.
Introduction:
We have previously worked with basic trigonometric ratios.
Today we will learn the sine rule which extends trigonometry to solve for sides and angles in any triangle.
Content:
The sine rule states that a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C, where a, b, c are sides and A, B, C are opposite angles.
This rule works for any triangle, not just right-angled ones.
For example, in triangle ABC with a = 7cm, b = 5cm, and angle A = 60°, we can find angle B using sin B = (b sin A)/a = (5 × sin 60°)/7 ≈ 0.618, so B ≈ 38.2°.
Bearings are measured clockwise from north and are often used with the sine rule.
In Nigeria, when traveling from Lagos to Abuja, the bearing might be given as 045° which means northeast.
Class activity:
Students will solve triangle problems using the sine rule, including those involving bearings.
Evaluation questions:
State the sine rule for triangle ABC.
In triangle ABC, a = 10cm, b = 8cm, and angle A = 50°. Find angle B.
A ship sails on a bearing of 060° for 20km, then on a bearing of 150° for 15km. How far is it from its starting point?
Find the length of side c in triangle ABC if a = 12cm, b = 9cm, and angle C = 60°.
Summary:
The sine rule is a powerful tool for solving triangles when we know certain sides and angles.

topics.title: Trigonometry: cosine rule
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the cosine rule.
The students should be able to apply the cosine rule to solve triangle problems.
Introduction:
We have previously learned the sine rule for solving triangles.
Today we will study the cosine rule which is useful when we know two sides and the included angle, or all three sides.
Content:
The cosine rule states that c² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C, where C is the angle opposite side c.
This rule works for any triangle and can be rearranged to find angles: cos C = (a² + b² - c²)/(2ab).
For example, in triangle ABC with a = 5cm, b = 7cm, and angle C = 60°, we can find side c using c² = 5² + 7² - 2×5×7×cos 60° = 25 + 49 - 35 = 39, so c = √39 ≈ 6.24cm.
Mixed triangle problems may require both sine and cosine rules.
In Nigeria, when determining the height of a mountain using trigonometry, we often need to apply multiple rules.
Class activity:
Students will solve various triangle problems using the cosine rule, including those requiring both sine and cosine rules.
Evaluation questions:
State the cosine rule for finding side c in triangle ABC.
In triangle ABC, a = 8cm, b = 6cm, and angle C = 120°. Find the length of side c.
Find angle B in triangle ABC if a = 7cm, b = 5cm, and c = 9cm.
A triangular plot of land has sides of lengths 20m, 25m, and 30m. Find the largest angle.
Summary:
The cosine rule is essential for solving triangles when we know two sides and the included angle, or all three sides.

topics.title: Circle theorems
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the circle theorems.
The students should be able to apply circle theorems to solve geometry problems.
Introduction:
We have previously worked with basic properties of circles.
Today we will explore circle theorems which help us understand relationships between angles, chords, and tangents in circles.
Content:
The angle at the center is twice the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc.
For example, if angle AOB is 100°, then angle ACB on the circumference is 50°.
Angles in the same segment are equal.
If angles ACB and ADB are both subtended by arc AB, then angle ACB = angle ADB.
The angle between a tangent and a radius is always 90°.
In Nigerian traditional architecture, circular designs often incorporate these principles for structural integrity.
Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to identify and apply circle theorems to solve geometry problems.
Evaluation questions:
State the theorem relating the angle at the center to the angle at the circumference.
In a circle, angle at the center is 120°. Find the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc.
If angle ABC is 45° and angle ADC is in the same segment, find angle ADC.
Prove that the angle between a tangent and a radius is always 90°.
Summary:
Circle theorems provide powerful tools for solving problems involving angles and lengths in circles.

topics.title: Coordinate geometry
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to calculate the gradient of a line.
The students should be able to find the midpoint of a line segment.
Introduction:
We have previously worked with basic algebraic expressions.
Today we will apply algebra to coordinate geometry which deals with points, lines, and shapes on a plane.
Content:
The gradient (slope) of a line is calculated as m = (y₂ - y₁)/(x₂ - x₁).
For example, the line passing through points (2,3) and (5,7) has gradient (7-3)/(5-2) = 4/3.
The midpoint of a line segment with endpoints (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂) is ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).
For instance, the midpoint between (1,2) and (5,8) is ((1+5)/2, (2+8)/2) = (3,5).
In Nigeria, when planning road construction, engineers use coordinate geometry to calculate gradients and midpoints for proper drainage.
Class activity:
Students will calculate gradients and midpoints for various line segments and then plot them on graph paper.
Evaluation questions:
Find the gradient of the line passing through points (3,4) and (7,10).
Calculate the midpoint of the line segment joining (2,5) and (8,9).
If a line has gradient -2 and passes through point (1,3), find its equation.
Show that points A(1,2), B(4,6), and C(7,10) lie on a straight line.
Summary:
Coordinate geometry allows us to analyze geometric shapes using algebraic methods.

topics.title: Revision and WAEC practice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to solve past WAEC questions accurately.
The students should be able to identify common errors in mathematics solutions.
Introduction:
We have covered various topics this term.
Today we will practice with past WAEC questions to prepare for the examination.
Content:
We will work through questions from previous WAEC mathematics papers.
Topics include indices, surds, quadratic equations, simultaneous equations, trigonometry, circle theorems, and coordinate geometry.
For example, a question might ask us to solve 2^x × 3^(x+1) = 108, which requires knowledge of indices and logarithms.
Another question could involve finding the area of a triangle using the cosine rule.
In Nigeria, WAEC exams are crucial for further education and career opportunities.
Class activity:
Students will work in groups to solve past WAEC questions and then present their solutions to the class.
Evaluation questions:
Solve the equation: log₂(x + 3) - log₂(x - 1) = 3.
In triangle ABC, angle A = 30°, angle B = 45°, and side a = 8cm. Find side b.
Find the equation of the line passing through points (2,3) and (-1,5).
A circle has center (3,4) and radius 5. Find the equation of the circle.
Summary:
Regular practice with past exam questions is essential for success in the WAEC mathematics examination.
